transcript:
Header: 2026-08-17 11:00 AM PT / Duration 50m
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood), Lena Brooks (Redwood), Carlos Vega (Redwood), Maya Chen (Novus), Jordan Lee (Novus), Priya Nair (Novus), Leo Park (Novus)
---
00:00 Samir Patel: Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, quick checkin — how's the staging replay been looking Maya?
00:23 Maya Chen: Uh thanks Samir. We ran the 24 hour replay with the baseline config, um p50 looks fine, p95 is around 360ms, p99s are kinda spiky 900 to 1.2s during the morning microburst window. Some of that is our front end batching too.
00:38 Lena Brooks: got it. When you say spiky, are those first-byte times or token stream stalls?
00:48 Maya Chen: mostly first-byte, we see long TTFB, the stream after handshake is okay. So the idea we talked about — priority queueing for short seqlens — seemed promising in our sim.
01:02 Jordan Lee: to add, our median sequence length is 28 tokens for the retail assistant use-case, but there's a long tail — 10% of requests are >250 tokens for receipts parsing which blows up cost and latency.
01:20 Samir Patel: right, that's classic. So two levers: route short seqlen traffic to a fastpath kernel and hedge or deprioritize larger seqlens. Also prefix KV caching for repeat prompts can knock down p50 a lot.
01:35 Maya Chen: yeah we enabled prefix cache but hit rates weren't great, I think because our prompt scaffolding varies per customer.
01:45 Carlos Vega: quick note — the KV cache effectiveness often depends on tokenization differences; small changes in prompt templating can reduce hits. We can run a cache-worthy pattern analysis.
01:58 Priya Nair: are we also looking at quantization tradeoffs here? We can't sacrifice accuracy too much for the receipts extraction.
02:06 Lena Brooks: absolutely. For short-response low-latency paths we typically use q4f16 on A100 and compare with q5_0 on H100 for the long seqlen model. Accuracy delta is small for our guarded prompts; but we need your eval set to be sure.
02:20 Jordan Lee: we'll provide an eval set, yes.
02:28 Samir Patel: good. Today I want to confirm the staging A/B: priority-queue flag on vs off, and a kernel-targeted vs generic path. If we see at least 20% improvement in first-byte p95 without pushing p99 for long requests above your SLA, we flip to canary.
02:44 Maya Chen: sounds reasonable. One question — how does the fastpath affect token throughput? Could we drop overall QPS?
02:51 Lena Brooks: no, the fastpath keeps throughput similar because it routes by policy: small seqlens get CPU/GPU scheduling priority; large seqlens run on a different worker pool or longer time-sliced kernels. It actually increases overall effective throughput because microbursts queue less.
03:10 Leo Park: real world concern — our ingress LB has short timeouts; if the first byte is delayed we see aborted requests on our side.
03:20 Samir Patel: yes that's the failure mode we're trying to fix. The priority-queueing target is to push first-byte under the LB timeout for p99.
03:28 Jordan Lee: you mentioned hedging earlier, can you explain the recommended hedging policy?
03:35 Lena Brooks: sure — for hedging we start a parallel hedged request to a replica with more headroom at ~90 ms if the client hasn't seen first-byte. That reduces tail but doubles some work; we recommend hedges only for critical short tasks.
03:50 Maya Chen: hedging sounds expensive though, we're cost-sensitive.
03:55 Carlos Vega: it's a tradeoff — the platform can run hedges only during high-value paths; or we can run dynamic hedging based on route and confidence score, so not blanket hedges.
04:08 Priya Nair: okay. On kernel selection — we saw your earlier note about continuous-batching windows causing TTFT regressions at very small seqlens. How do you tune that?
04:20 Lena Brooks: we tune the batching window and lower the batch latency SLO for the fastpath. Essentially we reduce the batching wait from 8 ms to 2 ms for short seqlens so first-token is generated quickly, but we also use kernel fusions that leverage smaller batch sizes efficiently.
04:36 Samir Patel: and on the runtime side we can pin the fastpath to a lower-latency kernel that uses optimized attention kernels for seqlen <= 64. We have profiles to show which kernels beat the others by seqlen and batch size.
04:50 Maya Chen: can you share those profiles?
04:54 Samir Patel: yes, I'll upload the kernel CSVs. They show A100 q4f16 vs H100 q5_0 and a third column for mixed-precision fused kernels.
05:04 Jordan Lee: please include the exact compiler flags — last time we tried something similar our infra team missed a flag and got different numbers.
05:12 Carlos Vega: will do. Also note that the handshake streaming changes require a small client-side timeout bump during the canary to avoid false aborts while we test.
05:24 Leo Park: noted. We'll modify the client timeout for the staging canary.
05:28 Samir Patel: great. Quick demo time — Lena, can you walk through the priority-queue rule config?
05:34 Lena Brooks: yeah, opening the doc — so the rule is simple: if request seqlen_predicted <= 64 and model_variant == fastpath-1 then route to fastpool, priority queue weight 10, preemptive scheduling enabled. The fallback is regular pool with hedging enabled after 90ms.
05:55 Maya Chen: how do we predict seqlen at ingress? We don't want to send actual user data.
06:02 Samir Patel: we use a lightweight tokenizer estimate on the client that returns seqlen bucket. That can be done client-side to avoid sending full prompt. Alternatively you can send a small hash-based fingerprint.
06:15 Jordan Lee: we'll try client-side estimate first.
06:18 Priya Nair: security check — does that require any PII to leave the VPC?
06:23 Samir Patel: no, the estimator runs locally. Only a small integer bucket crosses the wire. If you prefer, we can compute it with a private function in your VPC private deployment.
06:35 Maya Chen: good. One more thing — stream early token behavior. We saw some cases where the first token is emitted quickly but then there's a stall between token 2 and 3.
06:46 Lena Brooks: that's often due to KV cache warmup — the first token can be served from a tiny prefix, then we need to load KV shards for the rest, causing a pause. We can mitigate by eager prefetch of KV shards for predicted longer responses, or keep a small warmup background load for the fastpool.
07:06 Carlos Vega: also sequence-length aware kernel warmup helps — if we see a request predicted at >256, we spin up a worker with appropriate kernel to avoid cold start.
07:18 Jordan Lee: how much overhead is the warmup?
07:22 Lena Brooks: small — a few ms per warmed worker; the cost is amortized across concurrent requests.
07:27 Samir Patel: to keep this actionable: two experiments this week. Experiment A: priority-queueing on staging for 48h plus kernel profile attached. Experiment B: hedging disabled, but KV eager prefetch enabled for a 12h window to see effect on token stalls.
07:45 Maya Chen: ok we can run both A and B in parallel on separate subsets. We'll use morning traffic window for A and afternoon for B.
07:53 Samir Patel: perfect. Action items — I'll upload the kernel perf CSV and deck link. Also attaching a short runbook for the priority-queue flags. Shared: https://redwood.app/decks/novus-queueing-v1 and https://redwood.app/spreadsheets/novus-kernel-profiles.csv
08:12 Jordan Lee: about measurement — what exact metrics should we collect? We want to be able to compare apples to apples.
08:18 Lena Brooks: collect first-byte latency (ms), time-to-first-token (TTFT) p50/p95/p99, stream token interarrival p50/p95, KV cache hit rate, producer-side LB aborts, and cost delta per 1M tokens.
08:32 Leo Park: we'll also capture end-to-end client aborted request counts and backend error codes.
08:38 Maya Chen: one compliance quick ask — we need confirmation that enabling priority queueing doesn't change audit log semantics. Are request IDs preserved?
08:47 Carlos Vega: yes, request IDs are preserved and trace propagation remains the same. The route decision is logged as route_hint meta, which you can filter in the console.
08:57 Priya Nair: please send sample audit log rows so our compliance team can sign off.
09:02 Samir Patel: will do.
09:05 Maya Chen: any risks we should be aware of?
09:08 Lena Brooks: risk: misprediction of seqlen may route a long request to fastpath and degrade throughput. Mitigation: low-leak reclamation and immediate fallback; also canary against small % of traffic.
09:21 Jordan Lee: what's your recommended canary percent?
09:24 Samir Patel: start at 2% of traffic for 24h, if stable move to 10% for another 24h, then to 50% if numbers are good.
09:33 Maya Chen: will follow. One last Q — would switching to q5_0 on H100 for the fastpath help more than the scheduling changes?
09:41 Lena Brooks: in our profile H100 q5_0 beats A100 q4f16 for long seqlens but for very short seqlens the fused kernels on A100 actually win due to mem bandwidth characteristics. That's why we want to test both kernels in your staging traffic.
09:59 Priya Nair: ok that nuance is why we need the CSVs and the flags.
10:05 Samir Patel: wrap up — recap next steps: Samir upload artifacts, Lena enable priority-queue flag in staging and run microburst replay, Carlos upload KV hit breakdown, Novus provide traces and eval set and confirm SOC2 contact. We'll reconvene next Monday same time for results.
10:25 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll aim to have traces uploaded by EOD tomorrow.
10:30 Samir Patel: thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
---
Notes: Transcription contains occasional mislabels (Speaker 2 present). Some product names abbreviated. The conversation includes tradeoffs between hedging cost and latency SLOs, kernel profiles, and first-byte queue routing.
